LLM auditresponse for PKGBUILD:
<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
The PKGBUILD is a standard Python package wrapper for `python-google-genai`. The `source` array downloads a tarball from the official upstream repository at `https://github.com/googleapis/python-genai` (via the GitHub archive URL with a tagged release), which is the project's own declared upstream. The `sha256sums` array contains a proper SHA256 checksum (not SKIP), pinning the artifact to a specific known hash.

There is no `pkgver()` function, and the top-level/global scope of the PKGBUILD only contains variable definitions and array assignments — no command substitution, no `eval`, no network calls, no file exfiltration, and no obfuscated code. The `prepare()`, `build()`, `check()`, and `package()` functions are all out of scope for this narrow gate (they will not execute under `--nobuild --noprepare`).

Running `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo` will only fetch the verified tarball, extract it, and parse the PKGBUILD — all of which are safe.
</details>
<evidence></evidence>
<summary>Standard Python package PKGBUILD with official upstream source and valid checksum; safe for the narrow gate.</summary>
</security_assessment>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD appears to be a standard Arch Linux package for the python-google-genai SDK. The source fetches from the official Google APIs GitHub repository at a specific tagged version (v2.20.0), and the sha256sums checksum is provided (not SKIP). 

The `prepare()` function contains two `sed` commands: one removes overly restrictive version constraints from pyproject.toml (twine, packaging, pkginfo), and the other updates a deprecated `wait.initial` to `wait.multiplier` for tenacity compatibility. Both are routine packaging fixes to ensure the package builds with current dependency versions. The `build()`, `check()`, and `package()` functions follow conventional patterns — running the upstream build system, executing pytest (with many tests ignored/deselected that require API credentials), and installing the built wheel into $pkgdir respectively.

No suspicious network requests, obfuscated code, eval/base64 usage, or dangerous commands are present. The package's operations are confined to standard Python packaging workflows and do not exfiltrate data, download executables from unexpected hosts, or perform system modifications beyond supporting the application's stated purpose.
</details>
